title: I Still Don't Own a Pen
author: Michael G. Wagner
summary: Michael Wagner, a neurodivergent educator near retirement, uses his lifelong inability to take useful notes to challenge the popular slogan that writing is thinking. He traces the claim from Paul Graham and Leslie Lamport back to Janet Emig's 1977 essay, notes that Socrates made the opposite argument in the Phaedrus, and grants that a 56-experiment meta-analysis found writing moderately helps learning on average. He then argues that averages hide individuals: in nearly one in five studies, writers learned less. Drawing on Berninger's Not-So-Simple View of Writing, he explains how transcription competes with ideas for working memory, and on Messick's construct-irrelevant variance, he warns that essay grades can mix transcription with understanding. Citing research on visual, spatial and embodied thinking, he cautions against absolutism in either direction, applies the same logic to AI, and concludes that educators should ask who did the thinking rather than who held the pen.
points: Writing-to-learn has real evidence behind it, but an average effect conceals students for whom writing competes with thinking for limited working memory.

Essay-based assessment can measure transcription speed alongside understanding, which Messick called construct-irrelevant variance and which Universal Design for Learning tries to address by offering multiple ways to show knowledge.

Evidence on dyslexic, autistic and ADHD strengths in visual, perceptual and divergent thinking is real but thinner and more contested than popular accounts suggest, so neither deficit nor strength should be assumed.
The cockpit story of the 1950 Air Force study, where no pilot matched the average on ten dimensions, shows why rules built from averages fit no actual student.
AI can hollow out thinking for one student and give another access to ideas that were always theirs, so teachers should focus on who did the thinking.
quotes: I feel that I am living proof that this is not true, at least not for everybody.

If you put Thamus and Paul Graham side by side, their arguments are almost identical. Both warn that a new technology lets people skip the mental work and leaves them with only the appearance of understanding.
The people who shape a debate about thinking are usually the people who are best at the dominant medium of their time. So they experience that medium as the place where their own thinking happens.
An average describes a whole population. It tells you that, across many classrooms, writing helped more often than it hurt, but it tells you nothing about the one student sitting in the third row.
I think education research has the same problem whenever it turns an average into a rule. A finding like “writing improves learning” describes a student who doesn’t exist.

A student who lets a model write an essay about a topic they never thought about has skipped the work the assignment was meant for. But a student whose ideas used to get lost somewhere between their head and the page, and who can now get them out through dictation or a conversation with a language model, has gained access to thinking that was always theirs.
When I look at a student’s work, what I really want to know is who did the thinking. Whether they held a pen while doing it tells me very little about that.
A study that reports an average tells you something about a crowd, and you are not a crowd.
